[Q4 Attempt 1]

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child’s behavior was challenging for you. How did you approach it?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q10 Attempt 1]
Um, so I had a child, uh, last year that would have these really intense, angry outbursts and, um, you know, he would, it would become physical at times where, you know, he would throw objects or he would, you know, become really like physical if you tried to approach him. So what I had learned, what I had learned from him and his behaviors was that if I wasn't approaching him and if I wasn't giving attention to the behavior in the moment, um, then he would kind of deescalate on his own. I felt like the more that I was trying to get to him, then the more the situation would escalate. So I would just kind of tell him like, you know, case, and I'm going to give you your space over here for a minute. If you're upset, then you could be upset. This could be your, angry space. And when you're ready to come talk to me after you've had a few breaths and I would remind him like what we could do, like we could take a few breaths or I would offer to take him on a walk, you know, fresh air helps me feel better. Sometimes maybe that'll help you calm down as well. And usually he would just, you know, take a moment and would sit by himself. And, you know, it went from in the beginning where he was, you know, throwing objects to just when he would get upset, it just would come to him taking off. And then it got to the point where he wasn't doing any more of that at all, where he would just start taking the deep breaths and would kind of remove himself for a moment and then come back in the group when he felt that he was ready. And then, you know, I would have my director or an aide or someone else present with me in the room as well, you know, for backup, just in case.
